amil: مِنْ نَوَاصِبِ الْمُضَارِعِ — a governor (amil) that puts the following verb in nasb

explanation.en: أَنْ turns a verb into the equivalent of a masdar ("that he return" = "his returning") and forces the present verb into the subjunctive (mansub): a fatha replaces the final damma. In Birgivi's Awamil it is listed first among the four nasb particles: أَنْ، لَنْ، كَيْ، إِذَنْ. The whole clause then acts as a noun — in this story, أَنْ يَرْجِعَ is the object of أَرَادَ.

examples.en: You (pl.) must go — the نون drops: تَذْهَبُونَ → تَذْهَبُوا.

why.en: The damma stays by habit. After أَنْ the verb is mansub: fatha, not damma.
Confusing أَنْ (with verbs) and أَنَّ (with a following noun, from the إنّ family). Before a verb use أَنْ.
The five verbs (الأفعال الخمسة) mark nasb by dropping the ن — keeping it is a very common error.
